title: Themis convenes the assembly of the gods
greek: Ζεὺς δὲ Θέμιστα κέλευσε θεοὺς ἀγορήνδε καλέσσαι (Zeus de Themista keleuse theous agorēnde kalessai)
short: Themis, the goddess of right order and custom, is the fitting herald for a formal assembly of all the gods.
body: Themis personifies what is established and fitting: custom, right procedure, the order of things. In the Odyssey Telemachus appeals to Themis 'who dismisses and seats the assemblies of men' (Od. 2.68-9), and Leaf comments that the appropriateness of her role here is obvious. Her only other Iliadic appearance is in Book XV, where she greets Hera on Olympus (15.87-93). The summons is unusually wide: not only the Olympians but every river (except Oceanus) and every nymph of groves, springs and meadows comes, which makes this the fullest gathering of gods in the poem. The occasion is momentous because Zeus is about to lift the ban on divine intervention that he imposed at the start of Book VIII.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 20.4

title: Why Oceanus stays away
greek: οὔτε τις οὖν ποταμῶν ἀπέην νόσφ᾽ Ὠκεανοῖο (oute tis oun potamōn apeēn nosph’ Ōkeanoio)
short: Every river comes to Zeus' assembly except Oceanus, the world-encircling stream; ancient and modern critics have offered different explanations.
body: Oceanus is the great river that flows round the edge of the earth, source of all rivers and springs (21.195-7), and in one Homeric tradition the origin of the gods (14.201, 246). Leaf reports that the scholia give various reasons for his absence, and that Heyne thought the presence of rivers and nymphs at a council of the gods stranger than the absence of Oceanus, suggesting that lines 7-9 were added to account for the River Scamander's part in the coming battle of the gods (20.73-4; 21.211-382). Leaf also mentions the suggestion that Oceanus, the bond that holds the world together, cannot leave his place, as Hestia alone stays at home when the gods process in Plato's Phaedrus (247a). Whatever the reason, the exception emphasises how complete the gathering is.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 20.7 (citing Heyne and Plato, Phaedrus 247a)

title: Zeus releases the gods to fight
greek: ἀρήγετ᾽ ὅπῃ νόος ἐστὶν ἑκάστου (arēget’ hopēi noos estin hekastou)
short: Zeus lifts his ban on divine intervention: he will watch from Olympus while the other gods help whichever side they please.
body: At the start of Book VIII Zeus forbade the gods to help either side (8.5-27). Now he reverses the ban, giving a surprising reason: if Achilles fights alone, the Trojans will not hold him even for a moment, and he might sack Troy before its fated time. Zeus says he 'cares for' the Greeks and Trojans 'even though they die' (20.21); Leaf notes that the word for dying may apply to either side but shows that the Trojans are uppermost in his thoughts. Yet he also says he will sit in a fold of Olympus and 'delight his heart' watching, a phrase Leaf finds hard to square with that concern; it returns at 21.388-90, where Zeus laughs to see the gods clash. Leaf regarded this whole prologue as originally belonging to the battle of the gods in Book XXI and moved here to remove the veto of Book VIII before the gods intervened in the fight with Aeneas.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), Introduction to Book XX and notes on 20.21-26

title: 'Beyond fate' (huper moron)
greek: ὑπέρμορον / ὑπὲρ μόρον (hupermoron / huper moron)
short: Zeus fears Achilles may take Troy 'beyond what is fated': a Homeric idea that events can threaten to outrun destiny, and gods must prevent it.
body: Homer several times imagines things happening 'beyond fate' or 'beyond one's portion': the Achaeans would have sailed home huper mora if Hera had not intervened (2.155); the Achaeans prevail 'beyond their allotted share' (huper aisan, a close variant) as Patroclus attacks (16.780); Apollo fears they will sack Troy beyond fate (21.517); and Zeus complains that men like Aegisthus bring suffering on themselves 'beyond their lot' (Od. 1.34-5). Fate in Homer is not a mechanism that runs by itself; the gods see to it that it is fulfilled. Leaf records the ancient debate whether to write one word or two (Aristarchus and most grammarians preferred hupermoron), concluding that the sense is the same. He also notes that one ancient text replaced lines 29-30 with lines about the wooden horse, apparently because an all-knowing god ought not to fear what might happen.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 20.30

title: The gods take sides
greek: δίχα θυμὸν ἔχοντες (dicha thumon echontes)
short: A short catalogue sorts the gods: Hera, Athena, Poseidon, Hermes and Hephaestus for the Greeks; Ares, Apollo, Artemis, Leto, Xanthus and Aphrodite for Troy.
body: The division matches the gods' loyalties throughout the poem. Hera and Athena hate Troy since the Judgement of Paris (24.25-30); Poseidon was cheated by Laomedon (21.441-57); Hephaestus is bound to Thetis and Achilles; Hermes' role is less clearly motivated. On the Trojan side Aphrodite protects Paris and her son Aeneas, Apollo is the city's chief divine champion, and Artemis and Leto are his sister and mother; Xanthus is the local river. Hephaestus' limp (20.37) is noted with characteristic humour. Leaf finds no clear principle in the later pairings (20.67-74) except the opposition of fire and water in Hephaestus and Scamander. He also observes that the traditional title of the book, Theomachia, 'Battle of the Gods', is a misnomer: the clash is announced here but fought in Book XXI.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), Introduction to Book XX and note on 20.67

title: Phoebus akersekomēs, 'of the unshorn hair'
greek: Φοῖβος ἀκερσεκόμης (Phoibos akersekomēs)
short: Apollo's epithet 'with uncut hair' appears only here in Homer; long hair marks him as the eternal youth among the gods.
body: The compound joins a- ('not'), keirō ('cut, shear') and komē ('hair'). Leaf notes that it occurs only here in Homer and otherwise in the Homeric Hymn to Apollo (134) and Pindar and later poets. Greek boys wore their hair long until they came of age, when it was cut and often dedicated to a god (Achilles had vowed his to the river Spercheios, 23.141-51); Apollo, who never cuts his, remains forever on the threshold of manhood, the ideal kouros. The epithet suits the god of youths, music and archery who has been the Trojans' champion since Book I. Its rarity in Homer may suggest a cult or hymnic origin.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 20.39

title: Callicolone, 'Fair Hill'
greek: Καλλικολώνη (Kallikolōnē)
short: A hill near the river Simois from which Ares shouts to the Trojans and where the pro-Trojan gods later sit and watch.
body: The name means 'beautiful hill'. Homer mentions it only here and at 20.151, where Apollo and Ares sit on its brows while Poseidon's party sits on the wall of Heracles. Leaf remarks on the abrupt naming of a place as if it were well known. Strabo, following Demetrius of Scepsis, places Callicolone about ten stades above the 'Village of the Ilians', with the Simois flowing five stades away, and uses this passage in the ancient debate about where Homer's Troy stood: Ares' cries from the citadel and then from the Simois make sense, he argues, if the fighting was near the old site, whereas Callicolone is some forty stades from the later city of Ilium. The argument shows how closely ancient geographers read Homer's topography.

sources.cite: Strabo, Geography 13.1.35 (Loeb trans. H. L. Jones, 1928)
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 20.53

title: Aidoneus (Hades) leaps from his throne
greek: ἔδεισεν δ᾽ ὑπένερθεν ἄναξ ἐνέρων Ἀϊδωνεύς (edeisen d’ hupenerthen anax enerōn Aïdōneus)
short: As Zeus thunders and Poseidon shakes the earth, the lord of the dead leaps up in fear that his dark realm will be laid open: the cosmos itself trembles.
body: Aidoneus is a lengthened form of the name Hades. The passage builds a three-level picture of the universe: Zeus thunders above, Poseidon shakes the earth, Ida's peaks and the ships of the Greeks, and Hades below fears that the ground will split and expose his 'dread and dank' house, which even the gods loathe. A similar cosmic tremor shakes Hades in Hesiod's battle of Zeus and Typhoeus (Theogony 850). In the treatise On the Sublime (9.6-7), 'Longinus' quotes these lines, joined with 21.388, as an example of grandeur in which the whole universe is overturned, while observing that, taken literally, such stories about the gods are impious unless read as allegory. M. D. Usher discusses how Longinus uses these Homeric theomachy lines in his ninth chapter.

sources.cite: M. D. Usher, 'Theomachy, Creation, and the Poetics of Quotation in Longinus Chapter 9', Classical Philology 102 (2007), 292-303

title: The language of gods and men: Xanthus and Scamander
greek: ὃν Ξάνθον καλέουσι θεοί, ἄνδρες δὲ Σκάμανδρον (hon Xanthon kaleousi theoi, andres de Skamandron)
short: The Trojan river has two names, 'Xanthus' among the gods and 'Scamander' among men: one of Homer's few references to a divine language.
body: Homer occasionally gives a thing's name in the language of the gods beside its human name: the hundred-handed Briareus whom men call Aegaeon (1.403-4), the hill Batieia that the gods call the tomb of Myrine (2.813-14), the bird chalkis called kymindis by men (14.290-1), and the plant moly (Od. 10.305). Leaf, following his note on 1.403, suggests that both names might be attempts to render a foreign, hard-to-pronounce local name. Calvert Watkins placed the passages in a wider Indo-European tradition of contrasting divine and human vocabulary. Xanthus means 'tawny, yellow', perhaps from the colour of the water; Achilles' horse bears the same name. The river god will fight Achilles in Book XXI and be defeated by Hephaestus, the fire god he faces in this pairing.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 20.74
Calvert Watkins, 'Language of Gods and Language of Men: Remarks on Some Indo-European Metalinguistic Traditions', in J. Puhvel (ed.), Myth and Law among the Indo-Europeans (Berkeley, 1970), 1-17

anchor: went forth to meet with gods
title: The Theomachy, or battle of the gods
greek: ὣς οἱ μὲν θεοὶ ἄντα θεῶν ἴσαν (hōs hoi men theoi anta theōn isan)
short: The gods line up in pairs against each other, but the fighting is postponed to Book XXI; ancient critics were troubled and turned to allegory.
body: The pairs are Poseidon against Apollo, Athena against Ares, Hera against Artemis, Hermes against Leto, Hephaestus against the river Xanthus. The battle itself is delayed to 21.385-513, where it turns almost comic. Gods fighting gods offended ancient moralists: Plato excludes from his ideal city the 'battles of gods' that Homer composed (Republic 2.378d). One defence was allegory. Leaf reports, from Porphyry in the scholia on this line, that reading the gods as natural elements or qualities (Athena as wisdom, Aphrodite as desire, and so on) was very old and went back to Theagenes of Rhegium, who 'first wrote about Homer' in the late sixth century BC. This makes the scholion on Iliad 20.67 one of our oldest pieces of evidence for allegorical reading of Homer. Leaf thought the pairings had no principle except fire against water.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 20.67 (on Porphyry and Theagenes of Rhegium); Introduction to Book XX

title: Apollo disguised as Lycaon
greek: Λυκάονι δ᾽ υἷι Πριάμοιο εἰσάμενος (Lukaoni d’ huii Priamoio eisamenos)
short: Apollo, taking the voice of Priam's son Lycaon, goads Aeneas into facing Achilles; Lycaon himself will be killed by Achilles in the next book.
body: Gods in Homer often take the shape or voice of a mortal to speak to a hero (compare Athena as Deiphobus deceiving Hector at 22.226-47). Apollo reminds Aeneas of his boasts over the wine-cups that he would fight Achilles man to man, and argues from birth: Aeneas is the son of Aphrodite, daughter of Zeus, while Achilles' mother is the daughter of 'the old man of the sea', Nereus, a lesser deity. The choice of disguise carries dramatic irony. Lycaon, son of Priam and Laothoe, was once captured by Achilles and ransomed (21.34-48); in Book XXI he will meet Achilles again, beg for his life and be killed without mercy (21.64-135). The god speaks with the voice of a man whose doom is close.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 20.79-111

title: Achilles' raid on Ida, Lyrnessus and Pedasus
greek: βοῶν ἔπι … πέρσε δὲ Λυρνησσὸν καὶ Πήδασον (boōn epi … perse de Lurnēsson kai Pēdason)
short: Aeneas recalls an earlier encounter: Achilles drove him from his cattle on Mount Ida and sacked Lyrnessus and Pedasus, an episode told in the lost Cypria.
body: The story belongs to the years before the Iliad's action. Proclus' summary of the Cypria, the lost epic of the war's beginning, says that Achilles drove off Aeneas' cattle and sacked Lyrnessus and Pedasus and many neighbouring towns. Aeneas escaped, by his own account through the help of Zeus (20.92-3); Achilles mocks him for running without looking back (20.188-90). Lyrnessus, a town of the Leleges near Ida, is where Achilles captured Briseis (2.690-3; 19.291-6), so the two heroes' past is entangled with the quarrel that drives the poem. Strabo reports Demetrius of Scepsis' argument that Scepsis was Aeneas' royal seat, lying between his territory and Lyrnessus, and quotes these very lines.

sources.cite: Proclus, Chrestomathy, summary of the Cypria (in M. L. West, Greek Epic Fragments, Loeb, 2003)
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 20.96 (the Leleges of Lyrnessus)

title: Divine mothers: Aphrodite against Thetis
greek: ὃ δὲ χείρονος ἐκ θεοῦ ἐστίν (ho de cheironos ek theou estin)
short: Apollo argues that Aeneas, son of Aphrodite, Zeus' daughter, outranks Achilles, son of Thetis, daughter of the old sea-god Nereus.
body: Both heroes are sons of goddesses and mortal fathers, and the duel is framed as a contest of divine pedigrees. Apollo's argument is a debating point, and the poem soon refutes it: Thetis' son wears armour made by a god, and Poseidon must rescue Aeneas. Behind the claim lies a real hierarchy. Thetis is a sea-nymph, one of the fifty daughters of Nereus (Hesiod, Theogony 240-64), while Aphrodite in the Iliad is a daughter of Zeus and Dione (5.370-1), an Olympian. Aeneas makes the same point himself at 20.206-12, naming Anchises and Aphrodite, and adding that one pair of parents will mourn a son that day. Yet Aphrodite was humiliated when she tried to protect Aeneas in Book V (5.311-430), a reminder that rank on Olympus does not guarantee success on the battlefield.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 20.104-9 and 20.206-9

anchor: spun for him with her thread
title: Fate spinning the thread of life
greek: ἅσσα οἱ Αἶσα γιγνομένῳ ἐπένησε λίνῳ (hassa hoi Aisa gignomenōi epenēse linōi)
short: Hera says Achilles must later suffer what Aisa (Fate) spun for him with her thread at his birth: the ancient image of destiny as spinning.
body: Aisa, like Moira, means one's 'share' or 'portion'. Here she is pictured as a spinner who twists the thread of a person's life at birth. Leaf compares 24.209-10, where Hecuba says that powerful Moira spun this fate for Hector when he was born, and Od. 7.196-8, where Alcinous speaks of the 'heavy Spinners' (Klōthes) who spin a man's lot at birth. Hesiod names three Moirai, Clotho ('Spinner'), Lachesis ('Allotter') and Atropos ('Unturnable') (Theogony 217-19, 904-6), and the image passes into Latin as the Parcae. In the Iliad the metaphor often coincides with mortality: what is spun at birth is above all the time and manner of death, and Hera's words tie Achilles' moment of glory to his early end.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 20.128

title: 'Hard are the gods to look upon'
greek: χαλεποὶ δὲ θεοὶ φαίνεσθαι ἐναργεῖς (chalepoi de theoi phainesthai enargeis)
short: Hera's maxim: when gods appear openly in their true form, they are terrible and hard to face.
body: Homeric gods usually come to mortals disguised, or are recognised only as they leave. Hera fears that Achilles will be terrified if a god confronts him unannounced, and so proposes that the pro-Greek gods should stand by him. The adjective enargēs means 'visible, in plain view'. Leaf compares Od. 3.420, where Nestor says Athena came to the feast enargēs, and Od. 16.161, where Athena appears to Odysseus but not to Telemachus because the gods do not appear plainly to all; also Od. 7.201. He adds Virgil's echo, when Aeneas says he saw the god himself 'in clear light' (Aeneid 4.358). The line states a principle that runs through Greek religion and literature: a full divine epiphany is overwhelming and dangerous, as Semele learned.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 20.131 (citing Od. 3.420, 7.201, 16.161 and Aen. 4.358)

title: The wall of Heracles and the sea-monster
greek: τεῖχος ἀμφίχυτον Ἡρακλῆος θείοιο (teichos amphichuton Hēraklēos theioio)
short: Poseidon's party sits on the earthwork built for Heracles when he fought the sea-monster sent against Laomedon's Troy.
body: The allusion is to the first sack of Troy. Laomedon, Priam's father, cheated Poseidon and Apollo of their pay for building the city walls (21.441-57). Poseidon sent a sea-monster (kētos); to appease it Laomedon exposed his daughter Hesione, and promised his divine horses to whoever killed the beast. Heracles killed it from behind a rampart built for him by Athena and the Trojans, was cheated in turn, and sacked Troy (the sack is told in Il. 5.638-51; the sea-monster and Hesione are not in Homer's text and come from Hellanicus via the scholia and Apollodorus). Leaf notes that the scholia and Apollodorus (Library 2.5.9) cite the story from Hellanicus, and that the use of 'the monster' with the article implies a familiar tale. It is fitting that the pro-Greek gods should sit on a monument of Troy's earlier betrayal and destruction, while their opponents sit on Callicolone.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 20.145-47

anchor: like a lion, a ravening lion
title: Achilles as the wounded lion
greek: λέων ὣς σίντης (leōn hōs sintēs)
short: Achilles rushes at Aeneas like a lion that ignores the hunters until wounded, then lashes its flanks with its tail and charges, to kill or be killed.
body: Leaf calls this simile one of the most finished and finest in Homer, standing out from its context. It traces stages of a lion's response: indifference to the crowd of hunters, the wound from a young man's spear, the gathering of fury with open jaws and foam, the self-lashing tail, the glaring eyes and the final charge, 'whether he slay some man or himself be slain'. That last phrase fits Achilles, who knows he will die. Leaf records the old belief, reported by a scholion, that a lion has a sting under its tail with which it whips itself into rage, and compares the Hesiodic Shield of Heracles 430-1. Lucan imitates the image for Caesar at the Rubicon, where the Libyan lion stirs itself with the lash of its tail (Pharsalia 1.205-12).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 20.164 and 20.170

title: Aeneas and the kingship of Troy
greek: τιμῆς τῆς Πριάμου (timēs tēs Priamou)
short: Achilles taunts Aeneas: is he fighting in hope of inheriting Priam's throne, or for a grant of land? Priam has sons of his own.
body: The taunt touches a real tension in the poem. Aeneas belongs to the junior branch of the Trojan royal house, descended from Assaracus rather than Ilus (20.230-40), and in Book XIII he holds back because he is always angry with Priam, who did not honour him though he was brave (13.459-61). Leaf links this passage with the genealogy that follows and with that earlier note. Achilles also mocks the idea of a temenos, an estate 'cut off' for a hero as reward, like the one the Lycians gave Bellerophon (6.194-5) or the Aetolians offered Meleager (9.574-80). The sneer is ironic in light of Poseidon's prophecy later in the book that Aeneas and his descendants will indeed rule the Trojans (20.307-8).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 20.180

title: Aeneas' genealogy: the house of Dardanus
greek: πρῶτον μὲν Δάρδανον τέκετο νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς (prōton men Dardanon teketo nephelēgereta Zeus)
short: Aeneas recites his descent from Zeus through Dardanus, Erichthonius and Tros, showing that he and Priam share an ancestor and belong to two branches.
body: The line runs: Zeus, Dardanus (founder of Dardania on the slopes of Ida, before Ilios existed), Erichthonius, Tros. Tros has three sons: Ilus, whose line goes through Laomedon to Priam and Hector; Assaracus, whose line goes through Capys to Anchises and Aeneas; and Ganymedes, carried off by the gods to be Zeus' cupbearer (Zeus paid Tros for him with the divine horses of 5.265-7). Laomedon's other sons include Tithonus, the consort of Dawn (11.1). Leaf notes that the presence of Erichthonius, otherwise an Athenian hero, is startling, and reports Fick's view that the passage reflects Athenian claims of kinship with Troy when Athens was establishing itself at Sigeum about 610 BC, a claim Strabo records. Aeneas prefaces it all by saying that the tale is famous, and Aristarchus athetized 20.205-9 as unnecessary.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 20.205-9, 20.215 and 20.219

title: The mares of Erichthonius and the North Wind
greek: τάων καὶ Βορέης ἠράσσατο βοσκομενάων (taōn kai Boreēs ērassato boskomenaōn)
short: Boreas, in the form of a dark-maned stallion, sires twelve fillies so swift that they run over standing corn and the crests of waves without breaking them.
body: Erichthonius, richest of men, owned three thousand mares; the North Wind fell in love with them, took the shape of a stallion and fathered twelve fillies. Leaf notes that the belief that mares could be impregnated by the wind was widespread in antiquity (compare the Harpy Podarge, who bore Achilles' horses to the West Wind, 16.149-51), but that here it need be no more than a mythical way of expressing extreme speed. The image of running over the tops of the corn ears and the sea's breakers without harming them was imitated by Virgil for the warrior maiden Camilla, who could fly over the crop without bruising it and skim the waves without wetting her feet (Aeneid 7.808-11). Wealth in horses, the passage implies, is the mark of the Dardanian royal line.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 20.221 and 20.223

anchor: a ship of an hundred benches
title: Insults to sink a ship
greek: οὐδ᾽ ἂν νηῦς ἑκατόζυγος ἄχθος ἄροιτο (oud’ an nēus hekatozugos achthos aroito)
short: Aeneas says the two could trade so many insults that a ship with a hundred rowing benches could not carry the load.
body: The adjective hekatozugos, 'with a hundred thwarts', occurs only here. Leaf explains that it evidently means 'a ship bigger than was ever seen': Homeric ships are much smaller, the Boeotian ships in the Catalogue carrying a hundred and twenty men each (2.509-10), and a twenty-oared ship is already large (Od. 9.322). The hyperbole makes words into cargo, a heavy freight of abuse. It belongs to Aeneas' complaint that he and Achilles are talking 'like children' instead of fighting, a protest that comes, somewhat comically, after his own long recital of his genealogy. The image of speech as physical weight leads into the following lines on the endless field of words.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 20.247

anchor: Glib is the tongue of mortals
title: The 'pasture' of words and the scolding women
greek: στρεπτὴ δὲ γλῶσσ᾽ ἐστὶ βροτῶν … ἐπέων δὲ πολὺς νομὸς ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα (streptē de glōss’ esti brotōn … epeōn de polus nomos entha kai entha)
short: Aeneas' reflection on language: the tongue is 'twisting', words range over a wide pasture, and you hear back the kind of word you speak.
body: Leaf explains streptē as 'voluble', able to turn easily this way or that. The phrase epeōn nomos is obscure; Leaf suggests 'field of words', literally the pasture where words find their food, and notes the comparison with 'winged words', where speech is pictured as creatures flying from man to man. The proverb 'whatever word you speak, such you will hear' has a close parallel in Hesiod (Works and Days 721), as Leaf notes. Aeneas then compares the two heroes to women who quarrel in the street, saying things true and false in their anger. Aristarchus athetized these five lines (251-5) as untimely, since Aeneas has already said 'let us talk no more', and as unworthy of the speakers. Modern readers often see the self-conscious talk about talk as part of the episode's slow, deliberate pace.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 20.248, 20.249, 20.250 and 20.251-55

anchor: five layers had the crook-foot god
title: The five layers of Achilles' shield (20.269-72)
greek: πέντε πτύχας ἤλασε κυλλοποδίων (pente ptuchas ēlase kullopodiōn)
short: The gold layer stops Aeneas' spear; four lines explaining the shield's layers of bronze, tin and gold were condemned by Aristarchus and are usually thought spurious.
body: Line 268, 'the gold stayed it, the gift of the god', recurs at 21.165, and Leaf explains that the gold, as the most precious material, stands for the whole metal facing. Lines 269-72 then explain that the spear passed two layers but was stopped by the third, there being two of bronze, two of tin inside, and one of gold. Leaf calls them spurious, following Aristarchus: someone took the 'five folds' (ptuches) of the shield in 18.481 to be layers of different metals, whereas they were probably of oxhide, and the arrangement given is absurd, since the gold would be hidden in the middle, neither useful nor decorative. A scholion adds that some critics had already rejected the lines and some copies lacked them. The passage shows ancient editors reasoning about the physical logic of the text.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 20.268 and 20.269-72

title: Poseidon's prophecy: Aeneas will rule the Trojans
greek: νῦν δὲ δὴ Αἰνείαο βίη Τρώεσσιν ἀνάξει καὶ παίδων παῖδες (nun de dē Aineiao biē Trōessin anaxei kai paidōn paides)
short: Aeneas is fated to survive so that Dardanus' line does not perish; he and his children's children will rule the Trojans. The seed of Virgil's Aeneid.
body: Poseidon explains that Zeus has come to hate the race of Priam, but that Aeneas must escape so that the line of Dardanus, Zeus' favourite mortal son, will not die out. The same promise appears in the Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite (196-7). Many scholars, notably P. M. Smith, have argued that both passages were composed with an eye to a family of Aeneadae who claimed to rule in the Troad; Strabo reports that a royal family at Scepsis claimed descent from Aeneas (13.1.52-3). Others, including more recent commentators on the Hymn, are sceptical. Strabo and the scholia also record a variant, 'will rule over all', which they said was invented to flatter the Romans; Leaf notes that it left no trace in the manuscripts. Virgil translates the prophecy at Aeneid 3.97-8: 'hic domus Aeneae cunctis dominabitur oris, et nati natorum'.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 20.306 and 20.307
P. M. Smith, 'Aineiadai as Patrons of Iliad XX and the Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite', Harvard Studies in Classical Philology 85 (1981), 17-58

anchor: shed a mist over the eyes
title: Poseidon snatches Aeneas from death
greek: αὐτίκ᾽ ἄρ᾽ ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἐπ᾽ ἀχλὺν χεῦε (autik’ ar’ ophthalmoisin ep’ achlun cheue)
short: Though pro-Greek, Poseidon rescues the pious Aeneas, hurling him over the ranks; Achilles finds only his spear and concludes Aeneas too is dear to the gods.
body: The scene follows the Homeric pattern of the 'if not' rescue: Aeneas would have died had not Poseidon seen (20.288-91). It is surprising that the help comes from a god who favours the Greeks. Poseidon's reasons are both fate and piety: Aeneas is guiltless, suffering for others' quarrels, and 'ever gives acceptable gifts' to the gods (20.297-9). Hera, bound by an oath with Athena never to help Troy, leaves the choice to him (20.310-17). Aeneas has been rescued before, by Aphrodite and Apollo in Book V (5.311-18, 445-8). Poseidon advises him to avoid Achilles while he lives, since no other Achaean will kill him (20.332-9). Leaf saw the whole duel (20.75-352) as an independent 'Aeneid' inserted here, noting how mild and talkative Achilles is in it; others take the contrast with Achilles' following savagery as deliberate.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), Introduction to Book XX

title: Iphition of Hyde and the Lydian landscape
greek: Τμώλῳ ὕπο νιφόεντι Ὕδης ἐν πίονι δήμῳ (Tmōlōi hupo niphoenti Hudēs en pioni dēmōi)
short: Achilles' first victim, Iphition, comes from Hyde under snowy Tmolus in Lydia; Achilles' vaunt names the Gygaean lake and the rivers Hyllus and Hermus.
body: Iphition, son of Otrynteus and a Naiad, is the first man Achilles kills in his return to battle, and his death is marked by a vaunt that, cruelly, lists the landscape of home: the Gygaean lake, where his ancestral estate lies, the fish-rich Hyllus and the eddying Hermus. These are real features of Lydia, near Sardis; Leaf notes that Hyllus feeds the great Hermus, and that Tmolus and the Gygaean lake appear in the Trojan Catalogue (2.864-6). Some ancient scholars identified Hyde with the later Sardis. Strabo reports that some added a line naming Hyde to the Catalogue but says no place called Hyde could be found among the Lydians (13.4.6). The motif of the warrior dying far from a beautifully described homeland is frequent in the battle books.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 20.385, 20.390 and 20.392

title: The bellowing bull of Poseidon Heliconius
greek: ὡς ὅτε ταῦρος ἤρυγεν ἑλκόμενος Ἑλικώνιον ἀμφὶ ἄνακτα (hōs hote tauros ērugen helkomenos Helikōnion amphi anakta)
short: Hippodamas dies bellowing like a bull dragged round the altar of Poseidon of Helice; the simile may allude to the Ionian festival at Mycale.
body: Poseidon was worshipped as Helikonios at Helice on the Gulf of Corinth, a cult the Ionians, according to Pausanias, kept up after they were driven out by the Achaeans; Hera mentions gifts brought to Poseidon at Helice in 8.203. Herodotus (1.148) says the Panionion, the common sanctuary of the Ionian cities at Mycale, was dedicated to Poseidon Heliconius. Leaf notes that if the simile refers to that festival, it would point to a later, Ionian origin for the passage. He also quotes a scholion explaining that the god was thought to accept the sacrifice when the bulls bellowed, and to be angry when they were silent. Helice itself was destroyed by an earthquake and flood in 373 BC (Pausanias 7.24.6-12, 7.25.4). The comparison turns the human victim into a sacrificial animal.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 20.404

title: Polydorus, youngest son of Priam
greek: Πολύδωρον … Πριαμίδην (Poludōron … Priamidēn)
short: Priam's youngest and dearest son, forbidden to fight, shows off his speed among the front-fighters and is speared through the back by Achilles.
body: Polydorus' death is told with pathos: his father kept him from battle because he was the youngest and fastest, and 'in his folly' (nēpiēisi) he displays his speed until Achilles strikes him. In the Iliad his mother is Laothoe, daughter of Altes, king of the Leleges, and his full brother is Lycaon (21.84-91; 22.46-8); Strabo cites this as evidence for the Leleges' Trojan connection (13.1.7). Later tradition tells a different story: in Euripides' Hecuba, Polydorus is Hecuba's son, sent with gold to the Thracian king Polymestor, who murders him; Virgil follows this version when Aeneas finds Polydorus' grave in Thrace and the myrtle bleeds (Aeneid 3.19-68). His death here provokes Hector to come forward against Achilles (20.419-23).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 20.409

title: Three charges and a fourth 'like a god'
greek: τρὶς μὲν … ἀλλ᾽ ὅτε δὴ τὸ τέταρτον ἐπέσσυτο δαίμονι ἶσος (tris men … all’ hote dē to tetarton epessuto daimoni isos)
short: Achilles charges Hector three times into Apollo's mist and a fourth time 'like a god': the formula used before for Diomedes and for Patroclus' fatal attack.
body: Hector throws first, but Athena blows the spear back; Apollo snatches Hector away in mist. The pattern 'three times … but when the fourth time, like a god' recurs at decisive moments: Diomedes charges Apollo three times and is warned off (5.436-42), and Patroclus charges three times at the wall and three times into the Trojans before Apollo strikes him (16.702-11, 784-93). Leaf cross-references these passages and notes that line 447, with the phrase 'like a god' (daimoni isos), is missing in most manuscripts, though it occurs in all the parallels. For Patroclus the fourth charge was fatal; for Achilles it ends only in frustration and the insult 'dog' (20.449). Leaf praises Hector's frank admission just before that he is the weaker man (20.434-7).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 20.434 and 20.445-48

title: Tros clasps Achilles' knees: a supplication refused
greek: ὁ μὲν ἥπτετο χείρεσι γούνων ἱέμενος λίσσεσθ᾽ (ho men hēpteto cheiresi gounōn hiemenos lissesth’)
short: A young Trojan tries to clasp Achilles' knees and beg for life; Achilles kills him with a sword-thrust to the liver. After Patroclus, there is no mercy.
body: Supplication was a ritual: the suppliant touched the knees (and often the chin) of the stronger party and asked for mercy, often with an offer of ransom. Tros hopes Achilles will pity a man of his own age and take him alive. The narrator interjects 'fool!' (nēpios) and explains that Achilles was 'no sweet-tempered man, nor gentle of mind'. Leaf regarded the passage 463-8 as suspect, chiefly because the poet's comment on Achilles' character (467) is unlike epic style and the compound glukuthumos is strange; following Hentze, he also notes that the imperfect 'was touching' implies that Tros never completed the gesture. The scene prepares Lycaon's supplication in Book XXI, where Achilles explains that before Patroclus died he used to spare and sell captives, but now none will escape (21.99-113). The refusal of supplication marks the extremity of Achilles' grief until Priam clasps his knees in Book XXIV.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 20.463-69 (citing Hentze)

title: Achilles as a forest fire
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ἀναμαιμάει βαθέ᾽ ἄγκεα θεσπιδαὲς πῦρ (hōs d’ anamaimaei bathe’ ankea thespidaes pur)
short: Achilles rages everywhere like a wind-driven fire tearing through the glens of a dry mountain, and the black earth runs with blood.
body: The first of the two closing similes compares Achilles' rampage to fire in the deep valleys of a parched mountain, driven every way by the wind. Leaf notes that the verb anamaimaei, 'rages through', occurs only here, and compares Agamemnon's aristeia, where the Trojans fall like trees before a forest fire (11.155-9). Fire is the dominant image of Achilles in these books: his eyes blaze (19.16-17, 365-6), his head flames with Athena's fire (18.205-14), Hector says his hands are 'like fire' (20.371-2), and in Book XXI fire, sent by Hephaestus, will literally defeat the river that Achilles has choked with corpses. The phrase 'like some god' (daimoni isos) in 20.493 links the image to the divine scale of his violence.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 20.490

title: The threshing floor of corpses
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ὅτε τις ζεύξῃ βόας ἄρσενας εὐρυμετώπους τριβέμεναι κρῖ λευκόν (hōs d’ hote tis zeuxēi boas arsenas eurumetōpous tribemenai kri leukon)
short: Achilles' horses trample the dead as oxen tread barley on a threshing floor; the book ends with his 'invincible hands' spattered with gore.
body: The image comes from the farm: oxen yoked to tread out barley on a well-made threshing floor. Here the grain is dead men and shields, the axle and chariot rails are spattered with blood thrown up by hooves and wheels. The peaceful agricultural world, shown on Achilles' own shield (18.550-60), becomes a figure for slaughter, much as Odysseus' harvest metaphor did in Book XIX. Leaf reports that many editors rejected 495-503, partly because 499-502 repeat 11.534-7, and partly because Achilles, fighting on foot, suddenly appears in his chariot; Leaf replies that the borrowing is more likely in Book XI. The final line, 'his invincible hands' (cheiras aaptous) bespattered with gore, repeats Agamemnon's (11.169), closing the book on an image of defilement.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 20.495-503
